pages.text: After school in Kumasi, ten-year-old Kwaku loved watching Papa plane smooth odum wood in his carpentry workshop. One Friday, Papa glued four small offcut boards together, cut a narrow slot in the top, and handed the little wooden box to Kwaku. ‘This is your own susu box,’ said Papa.
sentences: After school in Kumasi, ten-year-old Kwaku loved watching Papa plane smooth odum wood in his carpentry workshop.
One Friday, Papa glued four small offcut boards together, cut a narrow slot in the top, and handed the little wooden box to Kwaku.
‘This is your own susu box,’ said Papa.
pages.alt: In a sunny Kumasi carpentry workshop, Papa hands Kwaku a small smooth wooden susu box with a coin slot on top.

pages.text: Every Saturday morning, Kwaku helped his Uncle Kofi arrange books at his stationery kiosk and earned five cedis. ‘Five cedis feels small when it is alone,’ said Maame that evening, ‘but when you make a budget, a plan for every cedi before you spend it, small amounts grow strong.’
sentences: Every Saturday morning, Kwaku helped his Uncle Kofi arrange books at his stationery kiosk and earned five cedis.
‘Five cedis feels small when it is alone,’ said Maame that evening, ‘but when you make a budget, a plan for every cedi before you spend it, small amounts grow strong.’
pages.alt: At the family table, Maame shows Kwaku how to divide five one-cedi coins into three small piles.

pages.text: Maame taught Kwaku to ask one question before buying anything: ‘Is this a need or a want?’ She explained, ‘A need is something essential for health, safety or learning—like food, clean water, medicine, or the fifteen-cedi geometry set you will need next term. A want is something fun to have, like a plastic spinning top or fizzy drink, that can wait.’
sentences: Maame taught Kwaku to ask one question before buying anything: ‘Is this a need or a want?’ She explained, ‘A need is something essential for health, safety or learning—like food, clean water, medicine, or the fifteen-cedi geometry set you will need next term.
A want is something fun to have, like a plastic spinning top or fizzy drink, that can wait.’
pages.alt: Kwaku draws two columns in his notebook showing a geometry set on one side and a spinning top on the other.

pages.text: Together they made Kwaku’s weekly five-cedi budget. Every Saturday, three cedis went straight through the slot of his wooden susu box for his geometry set. One cedi was for a small Saturday treat now, and one cedi went into a small envelope to share a gift for little sister Ama’s birthday.
sentences: Together they made Kwaku’s weekly five-cedi budget.
Every Saturday, three cedis went straight through the slot of his wooden susu box for his geometry set.
One cedi was for a small Saturday treat now, and one cedi went into a small envelope to share a gift for little sister Ama’s birthday.
pages.alt: Kwaku drops three one-cedi coins into his wooden susu box while setting aside two coins on the table.

pages.text: On Tuesday after school, Kwaku’s friends crowded around a street seller spinning glowing plastic tops for four cedis each. ‘Buy one, Kwaku!’ called his friend. Kwaku touched the coin in his pocket and remembered his susu box at home. ‘It looks fun,’ he said, ‘but I am saving for my geometry set first.’
sentences: On Tuesday after school, Kwaku’s friends crowded around a street seller spinning glowing plastic tops for four cedis each.
‘Buy one, Kwaku!’ called his friend.
Kwaku touched the coin in his pocket and remembered his susu box at home.
‘It looks fun,’ he said, ‘but I am saving for my geometry set first.’
pages.alt: Outside school, classmates watch a glowing spinning top while Kwaku smiles politely and keeps his hand on his pocket.

pages.text: The next week, heavy rains washed out the road from the timber mill. Because no wood lorries could get through, Papa’s workshop had to wait for timber, and the price of rice and cooking oil at the market rose. That evening, Maame and Papa sat down calmly with their household notebook.
sentences: The next week, heavy rains washed out the road from the timber mill.
Because no wood lorries could get through, Papa’s workshop had to wait for timber, and the price of rice and cooking oil at the market rose.
That evening, Maame and Papa sat down calmly with their household notebook.
pages.alt: While rain falls outside the window, Maame and Papa calmly review their household budget notebook together.

pages.text: Kwaku looked worried. ‘Papa, did we do something wrong because money is tight this week?’ Papa put a warm hand on Kwaku’s shoulder. ‘Never think that, Kwaku. Many families work hard every single day and still face tight weeks when rains stop deliveries, prices rise, or someone falls ill. Having less money is never a sign of bad character.’
sentences: Kwaku looked worried.
‘Papa, did we do something wrong because money is tight this week?’ Papa put a warm hand on Kwaku’s shoulder.
‘Never think that, Kwaku.
Many families work hard every single day and still face tight weeks when rains stop deliveries, prices rise, or someone falls ill.
Having less money is never a sign of bad character.’
pages.alt: Papa places a reassuring hand on Kwaku’s shoulder while Maame smiles warmly beside them.

pages.text: ‘What matters,’ said Maame, ‘is how a family plans together and cares for one another until the road opens again.’ By the sixth Saturday, the sun was shining, the timber lorry arrived at Papa’s workshop, and Kwaku had saved three cedis a week for six weeks.
sentences: ‘What matters,’ said Maame, ‘is how a family plans together and cares for one another until the road opens again.’ By the sixth Saturday, the sun was shining, the timber lorry arrived at Papa’s workshop, and Kwaku had saved three cedis a week for six weeks.
pages.alt: Sunlight shines on Papa’s workshop as Kwaku counts six weeks of tally marks beside his wooden susu box.

pages.text: With Papa’s help, Kwaku opened the base of his susu box and counted his savings: ‘Three, six, nine, twelve, fifteen, eighteen cedis!’ And in his sharing envelope, he had six cedis from the six weeks—enough to buy sweet roasted plantain and groundnuts for Ama’s birthday.
sentences: With Papa’s help, Kwaku opened the base of his susu box and counted his savings: ‘Three, six, nine, twelve, fifteen, eighteen cedis!’ And in his sharing envelope, he had six cedis from the six weeks—enough to buy sweet roasted plantain and groundnuts for Ama’s birthday.
pages.alt: Kwaku counts eighteen one-cedi coins on the table while little sister Ama claps happily.

pages.text: At Uncle Kofi’s shop, Kwaku paid fifteen cedis for his brand-new geometry set. Eighteen cedis minus fifteen cedis left three cedis! That night, Kwaku dropped the three remaining cedis back into his susu box to start his next goal. ‘Little by little,’ he smiled, ‘a good plan builds big things.’ The end.

activities.definition: A plan for how you will save, spend and share your money before you use it.

A game played at break time

activities.question: Which of these is a NEED rather than a want?
options: Medicine, food and a required school geometry set
activities.explanation: Needs are essentials required for health, safety and schooling; wants are nice to have but can wait.

activities.question: How did Kwaku divide his 5 cedis each Saturday?
options: 3 cedis to save, 1 cedi to spend, and 1 cedi to share
5 cedis to spend on spinning tops
4 cedis to spend and 1 cedi to save

activities.question: Why did Papa’s workshop have a tight week when the rains came?
options: Heavy rain blocked the timber road and prices rose, not laziness
Papa forgot how to make furniture
activities.explanation: External events like weather, road closures and rising prices affect hard-working families; tight money is never a sign of bad character.

activities.question: Kwaku saved 3 cedis a week for 6 weeks (18 cedis) and bought a 15-cedi geometry set. How much was left?

activities.prompt: Put Kwaku’s savings journey in order.
items: Papa builds Kwaku a wooden susu box from offcut wood.
Kwaku and Maame make a weekly five-cedi budget.
Kwaku passes up the spinning top to stick to his goal.
After six weeks, Kwaku buys his geometry set with three cedis left.

activities.prompt: Why is it important to treat every classmate with respect, no matter how much money their family has?
